title: The Ascension (Acts 1:6–11)
hook: he goes up and two men ask why they're staring at the sky

segments.voice: Yesterday, breakfast on the beach, and three questions by a charcoal fire. Your line was thou knowest that I love thee. Did you do the one kindness? Day seventy-two.

You've dropped someone at the airport. You've hugged, they've gone through security, and you're standing at the big window watching planes take off, not even sure which one is theirs. You keep looking anyway. Somebody has to tap you on the shoulder: you can't park here. For forty days after Easter, Luke says, the risen Jesus kept appearing to his friends. Then, on a hill called Olivet, just outside Jerusalem, it ends. He's lifted up, a cloud takes him out of their sight, and they stand there, eleven grown men, staring at the sky. Today's word is the name of that day.
screen: `STARING THROUGH THE AIRPORT WINDOW.` → `FORTY DAYS OF APPEARANCES.` → `A CLOUD TAKES HIM.`

segments.voice: Just before, they ask him a question that shows they still don't quite get it: "Lord, wilt thou at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel?" Is it now? Is this the moment? He doesn't answer the when. He gives them a job: they'll receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on them, and they'll be his witnesses in Jerusalem, and Judea, and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth. Then he goes up. And while they're still looking, two men in white stand beside them and say, in the Douay-Rheims: "Ye men of Galilee, why stand you looking up to heaven?" He'll come back, they say, the same way you saw him go. Ascension comes from the Latin for going up, climbing. But Catholics don't hear it as Jesus leaving the building. The Church teaches that he takes our human nature, wounds and all, into the life of God. Where he's gone, Catholics hope to follow. And the angels' question isn't a scolding, it's a nudge. Stop staring. You've got a job. So they walk back to Jerusalem, a Sabbath day's walk, and go to an upstairs room, and pray together, with Mary his mother among them, for about nine days. That's where the word novena comes from: nine days of prayer, and the first one was this wait. Catholics keep the feast forty days after Easter, a Thursday, though in many places it's moved to the following Sunday.
screen: `IS IT NOW? WRONG QUESTION.` · `WITNESSES, TO THE ENDS OF THE EARTH.` · `OUR NATURE TAKEN INTO GOD.` · `NINE DAYS: THE FIRST NOVENA.` · then, large: `WHY STAND YOU LOOKING UP TO HEAVEN?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look up, then get to work. Settle and breathe. If you can, look at the sky for a moment, or picture it. Let it be big. Let yourself hope, or wonder, or pray, whatever is honest. Then bring your eyes back down to the room. Think of one thing on your list today that you've been putting off, something that would help someone. Picture yourself starting it. If you pray, you can offer it to God. The bell holds the time.
Ascension. From the Latin for going up. Forty days after Easter, Jesus is taken up, and his friends are sent back down the hill to work. Today's word.
Your line: why stand you looking up. Today, catch yourself waiting for someday, and do the next small thing now. Day seventy-two.

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Ascension forty days after Easter (in many dioceses on the following Sunday), and many pray a novena, nine days of prayer, from the Ascension to Pentecost.

original.note: Latin: a going up, a climbing. from ascendere, to climb.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus floated away into space.
what it means: the Church says he takes our human nature into the life of God, and sends his friends back to work.
what a scholar hears: Luke tells it twice, at the end of his Gospel and the start of Acts, as a hinge between the two books. and the first novena is the nine days that follow.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Acts 1:6 and 1:11 given from memory; confirm.
The Ascension took place from Mount Olivet (Acts 1:12); Luke 24:50 says near Bethany. Script says 'a hill called Olivet'.
Novena origin: the nine days between Ascension and Pentecost are traditionally called the first novena. 'About nine days' allows for counting. Confirm phrasing.
Ascension Thursday transferred to the Seventh Sunday of Easter in most US ecclesiastical provinces and many countries. Confirm.
Ecclesiastical Latin pronunciation of ascensio given as ah-SHEN-see-oh. Confirm.
